newsitem.title: CANADA: AEC planning north Alberta oil pipeline.
newsitem.headline: AEC planning north Alberta oil pipeline.

text.p: Alberta Energy Co Ltd is joining the race to build pipeline capacity from Alberta's growing oil sands and heavy oil production with a line that would carry over 100,000 barrels per day, AEC chief executive Gwyn Morgan said on Wednesday.

"You could see an application filed for that fairly soon -- in the next few months," Morgan told reporters after AEC's annual meeting. "And then, from there, the exact timing will depend upon how quickly we can get customers for it."
Morgan said the project was being driven by the nearly C$6 billion worth of oil sands and heavy oil projects that have been announced in the northeast part of Alberta by numerous producers.
AEC already operates two pipelines in the area, one from the Cold Lake region and another from Canada's two main oil sands operations north of Fort McMurray.

He said the new line would likely flow to Hardisty, Alberta and could connect there with its own half-owned Express Pipeline to the U.S. Rocky Mountain region as well as IPL Energy Inc's Interprovincial Pipe Line.
Interprovincial and Suncor Inc have also said they planned to build major pipelines from the region.
Morgan said AEC had not decided on the size of the line, but he said it would have a capacity of over 100,000 barrels per day.
AEC, which earlier reported sharply higher earnings and cash flow for the first quarter, is targeting annual growth of 10 to 15 percent, Morgan said.
He said the company's natural gas sales were forecast to grow to 600 million cubic feet per day in 1997, up from 515 million in 1996.
Oil and gas liquids sales, including AEC's share of output from the Syncrude Canada Ltd oil sands operation, were expected to rise to 65,000 barrels per day from 53,000 barrels per day last year.
Of the C$600 million AEC has budgeted for exploration and production this year, about C$70 million was earmarked to fund operations in Argentina, Peru, Trinidad and Thailand, he said.
Another five percent of the budget would be used by a new exploration team to drill five to 10 high-risk, high-impact deep natural gas wells in Canada, he said.

Amid a series of rosy results and a strong outlook for the company, one sour note was the company's finding and development costs, which rose in 1996 to C$6.21 per barrel of oil equivalent from C$5.88 in 1995.

The increase was a result of major spending during the year to amass exploration lands in western Canada and build processing facilities, he said, adding that the company's F&D cost target was C$5 per BOE.

Morgan said he was relieved the bulk of the land expenditures were made last year when the average Canadian land sale price was C$169.23 per hectare, not this year as hot competition has pushed the price to C$286.52 per hectare.
